texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Abstract
texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Background :  Appendicular  abscess  represents  a  complex  manifestation  of  appendicitis,  traditionally managed  with  emergency  surgery  or  initial  conservative  treatment.  Minimally  invasive  percutaneous drainage combined with antibiotics has emerged as an alternative, potentially reducing morbidity.
texts.text: Background :  Appendicular  abscess  represents  a  complex  manifestation  of  appendicitis,  traditionally managed  with  emergency  surgery  or  initial  conservative  treatment.  Minimally  invasive  percutaneous drainage combined with antibiotics has emerged as an alternative, potentially reducing morbidity.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Objectives: This study aimed to compare clinical outcomes, postoperative recovery, and complications between surgical and percutaneous management of appendicular abscess.
texts.text: Objectives: This study aimed to compare clinical outcomes, postoperative recovery, and complications between surgical and percutaneous management of appendicular abscess.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients  and  methods :  A  prospective  cohort  study  was  conducted  at  Qena  University  Hospitals  from August  2024  to  August  2025,  including  53  adults  with  radiologically  confirmed  appendicular  abscess. Patients  were  allocated  to  surgical  drainage  (n  =  31)  or  ultrasound-guided  percutaneous  drainage  with antibiotics (n = 22). Allocation was by surgical team and based on patient selection and predefined clinical and  radiological  criteria.  Preoperative  assessment  included  clinical  evaluation,  laboratory  tests,  and imaging.  Procedural  details,  drain  management,  hospital  stay,  time  to  oral  intake,  complications,  and readmissions were recorded.
texts.text: Patients  and  methods :  A  prospective  cohort  study  was  conducted  at  Qena  University  Hospitals  from August  2024  to  August  2025,  including  53  adults  with  radiologically  confirmed  appendicular  abscess. Patients  were  allocated  to  surgical  drainage  (n  =  31)  or  ultrasound-guided  percutaneous  drainage  with antibiotics (n = 22). Allocation was by surgical team and based on patient selection and predefined clinical and  radiological  criteria.  Preoperative  assessment  included  clinical  evaluation,  laboratory  tests,  and imaging.  Procedural  details,  drain  management,  hospital  stay,  time  to  oral  intake,  complications,  and readmissions were recorded.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Results: The  median  patient  age  was  35(16-72)  years,  with  56.6%  male.  Percutaneous  drainage  was associated with significantly shorter operative time(100(55-160) vs. 15(7-45) min; p < 0.001), earlier drain removal(4(2-14) vs. 2(2-5) days; p=0.002), reduced hospital stay(5(3-17) vs. 3(2-7) days; p=0.002), and faster resumption of oral intake(4(4-6) vs. 24(24-48) h; p < 0.001). Postoperative complications, particularly wound-related events, were significantly lower in the percutaneous group(p < 0.001). Readmission rates were higher after percutaneous drainage(50%) for elective interval appendectomy.
texts.text: Results: The  median  patient  age  was  35(16-72)  years,  with  56.6%  male.  Percutaneous  drainage  was associated with significantly shorter operative time(100(55-160) vs. 15(7-45) min; p < 0.001), earlier drain removal(4(2-14) vs. 2(2-5) days; p=0.002), reduced hospital stay(5(3-17) vs. 3(2-7) days; p=0.002), and faster resumption of oral intake(4(4-6) vs. 24(24-48) h; p < 0.001). Postoperative complications, particularly wound-related events, were significantly lower in the percutaneous group(p < 0.001). Readmission rates were higher after percutaneous drainage(50%) for elective interval appendectomy.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conclusion: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics offers faster recovery and lower wound morbidity than surgical drainage for appendicular abscess, though some patients may still require interval appendectomy.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Introduction
texts.text: Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Appendicitis is a leading cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgical intervention (Brown et al., 2012;  Das  et  al.,  2019). In  2 -7%  of  cases, appendicitis presents with more complex manifestations, including abscess or inflammatory mass formation (Lind, 2019).
texts.text: Appendicitis is a leading cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgical intervention (Brown et al., 2012;  Das  et  al.,  2019). In  2 -7%  of  cases, appendicitis presents with more complex manifestations, including abscess or inflammatory mass formation (Lind, 2019).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Emergency surgical intervention in these patients is  often  avoided  due  to  increased  risks,  such  as widespread intra-abdominal inflammation, intestinal  adhesions,  postoperative  sepsis,  and delayed wound healing (Thomson et al., 2015). Consequently, several authors have recommended initial conservative management, including ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage combined  with  antibiotic  therapy,  followed  by interval appendectomy when indicated (Habib et al., 2018) . Evidence suggests that the recurrence rate  after  successful  conservative  treatment  is approximately 7%, indicating that interval appendectomy  may  not  be  routinely  required (Darwazeh et al., 2016).

Evidence suggests that the recurrence rate  after  successful  conservative  treatment  is approximately 7%, indicating that interval appendectomy  may  not  be  routinely  required (Darwazeh et al., 2016).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This  study  was  conducted  to  compare  clinical outcomes,  postoperative  morbidity,  and  hospital stay in patients managed with emergency surgery versus  those  treated  with  percutaneous  drainage for appendicular abscess.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This was a prospective cohort study conducted to compare  surgical  and  non-surgical  management of appendicular abscesses. The study was performed at Qena University Hospitals, encompassing  both the General Surgery and Radiology  Departments.  Patients  were  recruited from  the  hospital's  emergency  room  between August 1, 2024, and August 1, 2025.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Inclusion Criteria
texts.text: Inclusion Criteria

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients  were  eligible  for  inclusion  if  they  were adults presenting with a clinically and radiologically confirmed  appendicular abscess and able to provide informed consent. Suitability for either surgical drainage or ultrasound-guided percutaneous  drainage  was  determined  by  the treating surgical team based on patient selection and predefined clinical  and radiological criteria, including abscess size, location, complexity (e.g., multiloculated collections), presence of generalized peritonitis, patient comorbidities, and overall operative risk.
texts.text: Patients  were  eligible  for  inclusion  if  they  were adults presenting with a clinically and radiologically confirmed  appendicular abscess and able to provide informed consent. Suitability for either surgical drainage or ultrasound-guided percutaneous  drainage  was  determined  by  the treating surgical team based on patient selection and predefined clinical  and radiological criteria, including abscess size, location, complexity (e.g., multiloculated collections), presence of generalized peritonitis, patient comorbidities, and overall operative risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients  were  excluded  if  suspected  of  having underlying ileocecal disease or malignancy, had contraindications to anesthesia or antibiotic therapy, or if they declined to provide informed consent. Also, the immunocompromised patients and patients on cortisone or on immunosuppressive  drugs  were  excluded  from the study.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Preoperative Assessment
texts.text: Preoperative Assessment

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All participants underwent a detailed preoperative assessment.  Patient  history  included  symptom onset,  duration,  and  prior  medical  or  surgical conditions. Comprehensive physical examination assessed  vital  signs,  abdominal  tenderness,  and signs of localized or systemic infection. Laboratory investigations included complete blood count (CBC), random blood glucose, renal function tests (blood urea and creatinine), coagulation profile (prothrombin time and concentration),  CRP,  electrolytes,  and  screening for  infectious  diseases  (HBsAg,  anti-HCV,  HIV antibody).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Diagnostic imaging included erect abdominal Xrays to rule out perforation or obstruction, ultrasonography to confirm abscess size and location,  and  CT  scans  in  selected  cases  for detailed evaluation.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Patient Allocation and Management
texts.text: Patient Allocation and Management

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients were allocated into two groups based on treatment modality: Group A underwent surgical drainage,  and  Group  B  received  percutaneous drainage with interventional radiology and antibiotics. Patients were allocated to either group with the process standardized in the study protocol to ensure consistency and minimize selection bias.
texts.text: Patients were allocated into two groups based on treatment modality: Group A underwent surgical drainage,  and  Group  B  received  percutaneous drainage with interventional radiology and antibiotics. Patients were allocated to either group with the process standardized in the study protocol to ensure consistency and minimize selection bias.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Surgical Drainage (Group A): Surgical procedures were performed under general anesthesia  via  a  McBurney  or  right  paramedian incision.  The  abscess  was  evacuated,  the  cavity lavaged,  and  an  appendectomy  performed  when feasible. Drains (20 French) were inserted, anchored, and wounds closed. Daily drain output, wound  inspection,  and  dressing  changes  using povidone-iodine were recorded until discharge.

texts.orig: Postoperative and Follow-Up
texts.text: Postoperative and Follow-Up

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Postoperative care included monitoring the length of hospital stay, time to symptom resolution, and tolerance of oral feeding. Patients were assessed daily  for  fever,  leukocytosis,  and  drain  output. Ultrasound  evaluations  were  performed  every other  day  or  as  indicated.  Criteria  for  operative drain or catheter removal included minimal output (<5  ml  serous  fluid  for  three  consecutive  days) and ultrasound confirmation of complete abscess evacuation.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Results
texts.text: Results

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A total of 53 patients with appendicular abscess were included, with a median age of 35 (16 - 72) years; 30 (56.6%) were male and 23 (43.4%) were female.  At  admission,  systolic  (120  (90  -  150) mmHg) and diastolic (80 (60 - 100) mmHg) blood pressures were within the normal range. Respiratory rate was slightly elevated at 21 (17 26) cycles/min, whereas oxygen saturation remained  normal  (0.97  (0.94  -  0.99)  %).  The median temperature was mildly elevated at 38.1 (37.5 - 40) °C, with a corresponding increase in heart  rate  (96  (78  -  120)  bpm).  The  median duration of pain before admission was 5 (3 - 20) days. Laboratory findings showed marked leucocytosis  (12700  (4300  -  50000)/ μL),  with neutrophilia  (82  (67.3  -  96)  %)  and  relative lymphopenia  (14.6  (2.5  -  25)  %),  yielding  an elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (5.5 (3 38.4)).  Haemoglobin  (12.4  (10.7  -  14.1)  g/dL), renal  function  tests  (blood  urea  30  (15  -  43) mg/dL; serum creatinine 0.9 (0.3 - 1.3) mg/dL), and electrolytes (sodium 135 (122 - 144) mEq/L) were within normal limits, although serum albumin was mildly reduced (3.5 (2 - 4.6) g/dL). Inflammatory  markers  were  markedly  elevated, including ESR at 119 (50 - 200) mm/hr (first hour) and 65 (30 - 90) mm/hr (second hour), C-reactive protein at 150 (48 - 384) mg/L, and CRP/albumin ratio at 42.8 (10.4 - 97.1) The mean abscess size was 4.5 ± 1.4 cm with range (2 -10). (Table 1). Appendectomy  was  performed  in  all  patients managed surgically (31  [100%]) compared with 13  (59%)  in  the  percutaneous  group  (p  <  .001) (Fig 3).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Management  of  appendicular  abscess  remains controversial. Traditionally, conservative treatment  with  antibiotics  followed  by  interval appendectomy  was  recommended  to  avoid  the risks of early surgery, such as fecal fistula (Khorshid et al. 2022) However, the necessity of interval  appendectomy  has  been  questioned,  as conservative  treatment  can  fail  in  10 -20%  of cases,  requiring  emergency  surgery  with  higher morbidity, and recurrence may occur after discharge (Gignoux  et  al.,  2018). Increasing evidence supports nonsurgical approaches such as antibiotics combined with image-guided percutaneous  drainage,  which  have  shown  high success  rates  and  low  complication  incidence (Sekine et al., 2021).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In this context, this study compared the outcomes of ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage versus  surgical  drainage  in  patients  presenting with appendicular abscess. Overall, percutaneous drainage was associated with shorter hospital stay, earlier return to oral feeding, faster resolution of fever,  and  lower  readmission  rates  compared  to surgical management. These findings support the growing evidence that minimally invasive approaches  can  provide  effective  source  control with less morbidity  in appropriately selected patients.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The demographic profile of our study population, with a median age of 35 (16 - 72) years and a male predominance (56.6%), aligns well with the established epidemiology of complicated appendicitis.  This  age  distribution  is  consistent with previous reports, such as Mejri et al. (2021). The median duration of abdominal pain prior to presentation  was  5  (3  -  20)  days,  reflecting  the typical  delayed  presentation  that  favors  abscess formation.  On admission, patients demonstrated a moderate systemic inflammatory response, with elevated WBC count (12700 (4300 - 50000) / μL ) and fever (38.1 (37.5 -40) °C). Similarly, inflammatory  markers  were  markedly  elevated, with CRP averaging 150 (48 - 384) mg/L and ESR 65 (30 - 90) mm/hr. These findings are in line with previous  descriptions  of  localized  appendiceal perforation and abscess formation (Beltrán, 2015; Singh et al., 2024).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our  study  demonstrated  significant  differences between percutaneous drainage and surgical management  of  appendicular  abscess  in  both procedural  and  clinical  outcomes.  Percutaneous drainage was associated with significantly shorter procedure times (15 (7 - 45) vs. 100 (55 - 160) minutes,  p  <  0.001),  reflecting  the  minimally invasive  nature  of  image-guided  interventions. Similar  results  were  observed  by Negm  et  al. (2024) , who noted reduced operative durations in patients treated with conservative therapy.

texts.orig: Drain management  also  differed significantly between groups. Daily drain output was higher in the percutaneous cohort (140 (10 - 250) vs. 90 (60 -  200)  mL/day,  p  <  0.001),  which  may  indicate more effective evacuation of abscess contents via the pigtail catheter or differences in abscess cavity characteristics. Despite higher output, drains were removed earlier in the percutaneous group (2 (2 5) vs. 4 (2 - 14) days, p = 0.002), suggesting more rapid resolution of the infectious process. While some prior studies have suggested longer drainage periods for percutaneous approaches (Chaiyasoot and Jaruthien, 2021). Our findings likely reflect the specific image-guided technique and tailored antibiotic regimen employed.

texts.orig: Percutaneous drainage also conferred clear clinical advantages. Hospital stay was significantly shorter in the percutaneous group (3 (2 - 7) vs. 5 (3 - 17) days, p = 0.002), reflecting faster recovery and reduced postoperative burden. Oral feeding was resumed markedly earlier (4(4 6) vs. 24 (24 - 48) hours, p < 0.001), consistent with  minimal  bowel  manipulation  and  reduced systemic inflammatory response. Fever resolved in all percutaneous cases compared with 90.3% of surgical cases, with a shorter duration (3 (2 - 3) vs 2  (1  -  2)  days,  p  <  0.001),  indicating  more effective source control. These findings are supported by prior studies reporting rapid clinical improvement  with  percutaneous  drainage  when combined  with appropriate antibiotic therapy (Akingboye et al., 2021)

(2018) emphasized reduced morbidity and quicker functional recovery with conservative management compared to emergency appendectomy, highlighting how patient selection, timing, and institutional protocols may influence outcomes.

texts.orig: Residual collections on ultrasound before discharge were observed in both groups, though their  management  differed.  In  the  percutaneous group,  residual  collections  were  addressed  with catheter  reinsertion  (2  cases)  or  conversion  to surgery (2 cases). In the surgical group, 7 patients were managed conservatively with antibiotics, 4 patients required  ultrasound-guided  aspiration, and  2  patients  underwent  pigtail  insertion.  Our results are in agreement with Demetrashvili et al. (2019), who reported significantly fewer postoperative complications in patients managed conservatively with interval surgery compared to those undergoing emergency surgery (P = 0.02). Similarly, Habib  et  al.  (2018) demonstrated lower complication rates, including wound infection and dehiscence, in patients treated with ultrasound-guided drainage compared to emergency  appendectomy. Olsen  et  al.  (2014) further support these findings, showing that complications  such  as  wound  infection,  fecal fistula,  and  burst  abdomen  were  significantly more  frequent  in  surgically  managed  patients, whereas the percutaneous group experienced no major complications. Together, these data strongly support the safety advantage of percutaneous  drainage  over  surgical  drainage  in appendiceal abscess.

texts.orig: An important observation in our cohort was the higher readmission rate in the percutaneous group (50.0% vs. 19.4%, p = 0.019), predominantly for elective interval appendectomy. This reflects current  standard  practice,  where  percutaneous drainage serves as a bridge to delayed appendectomy, allowing resolution of acute inflammation.  Notably,  40.9%  of  percutaneous patients  had  atrophied  appendices  that  did  not require surgery, indicating that conservative management  can  be  definitive  in  a  substantial proportion  of  cases.  These  results  align  with previous studies, show high technical and clinical success rates for percutaneous drainage (Brown et  al.,  2012;  Habib  et  al.,  2018) ,  and  support selective, rather than routine, interval appendectomy.

texts.orig: Limitations & Recommendations: This study has some  limitations  that  should  be  acknowledged. First,  it  was  conducted  at  a  single  center  with  a relatively small sample size, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. Second, the nonrandomized design may introduce the possibility of selection bias in treatment allocation. Additionally, follow-up duration was limited, and thus long-term outcomes such as recurrence, late complications,  and  quality  of  life  could  not  be fully assessed.

Additionally, follow-up duration was limited, and thus long-term outcomes such as recurrence, late complications,  and  quality  of  life  could  not  be fully assessed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Future research should aim to address these gaps. Larger,  multicenter  randomized  controlled  trials are needed to confirm the superiority of percutaneous  drainage  over  immediate  surgical drainage  in  selected  patients  with  appendicular abscess. A longer follow-up is also warranted to better  evaluate  recurrence  rates  and  long-term morbidity. Moreover,  standardized  criteria  for patient selection between percutaneous and surgical  management  should  be  developed  to optimize outcomes and reduce variability in practice.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conclusion: Our findings suggest that ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage combined with antibiotics may offer advantages over surgical drainage for appendicular abscesses, including shorter hospital stay, earlier resumption of oral intake, and lower wound-related complications.  While  percutaneous  management appears effective in achieving abscess resolution, some patients still require elective interval appendectomy.
